s0.why: 5 defines a lava flow as an outpouring of lava in an effusive eruption and contrasts explosive eruptions producing ash and fragments.

s1.why: 2 gives 800 to 1,200 C, 5 the ketchup-like viscosity, 6 the insulating solid crust that lets lava flow great distances.

s2.why: 19 says high-silica lava is much more viscous, 23 calls felsic lavas extremely viscous, 40 says less viscous mafic lava flows far and builds low-profile shields; basalt for mafic is naming only.

f0.why: 2 says lava usually erupts at 800 to 1,200 C.

f1.why: 5 gives viscosity about that of ketchup, roughly 10,000 to 100,000 times that of water.

f2.why: 7 says the word comes from Italian and originally described a stream caused by sudden rain.

f3.why: 21 says felsic lavas have silica content greater than 63%.

q1.why: 6 says lava exposed to air quickly develops a solid crust that insulates the liquid and keeps it hot enough to keep flowing.

q2.why: 19 says high-silica lava is much more viscous than low-silica lava and 40 says less viscous lava flows long distances from the vent.

q3.why: 5 says most molten lava has about the viscosity of ketchup, 10,000 to 100,000 times that of water.

q4.why: 25 says very viscous felsic lavas usually erupt explosively to produce pyroclastic, fragmental deposits; the stem supplies the sticky, silica-rich premise.

q5.why: 43 says underwater these basaltic lavas can form pillow lavas resembling some pahoehoe on land.

q6.why: 41 says a solidified basalt flow can be much thicker than the moving flow because continued lava supply presses on the solid crust and inflates it.
